title: Baseline monocyte GIP receptor mRNA expression is associated with reductions in body weight and FIB-4 index after switching to tirzepatide in patients with type 2 diabetes.
abstract: Tirzepatide improves body weight and glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes, but factors associated with inter-individual differences after switching remain unclear. We examined whether baseline monocyte glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor (GIPR) mRNA expression was associated with changes in body weight and the fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) index after switching from glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) to tirzepatide. This single-center retrospective study included 90 patients with type 2 diabetes who had received a GLP-1RA for at least 6 months before switching. Baseline monocyte GIPR mRNA expression was measured by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction. Associations with percentage body-weight change and FIB-4 index change during the 6 months after tirzepatide initiation were assessed by correlation and multivariable regression. Exploratory ex vivo assays were performed to assess monocyte responses to native GIP. Higher baseline monocyte GIPR mRNA expression was associated with greater reductions in body weight and the FIB-4 index and remained significant in multivariable models. The association with the FIB-4 index remained significant after additional adjustment for percentage body-weight change at 6 months after tirzepatide initiation. GIPR mRNA expression was not associated with body-weight change during the preceding 6 months of GLP-1RA therapy. Native GIP suppressed lipopolysaccharide-induced interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha responses in monocytes. Baseline monocyte GIPR mRNA expression was associated with body-weight and FIB-4 index reductions after switching to tirzepatide. It may represent an exploratory marker of clinical changes, but treatment specificity, causal GIPR-dependent mechanisms, and structural liver fibrosis regression were not established. Summary of the study design and main finding. Baseline GIPR mRNA expression in peripheral blood monocytes was associated with reductions in body weight and the FIB-4 index after switching to tirzepatide in patients with type 2 diabetes. In exploratory ex vivo assays, native GIP suppressed LPS-induced inflammatory responses, supporting monocyte GIPR expression as a candidate exploratory marker requiring further validation. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13340-026-00940-3.

title: Ensemble-Based Segmental Helical Organization in an Aib-Rich Lipidated Peptide: Biomacromolecular Insights from High-Field NMR.
abstract: Tirzepatide (TZP) is a dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist that has demonstrated remarkable therapeutic efficacy for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity. Despite its clinical importance, residue-specific information on its solution conformation remains limited due to its structural complexity, including noncanonical amino acids and a lipidated side chain. In this study, we performed a solution NMR investigation of tirzepatide to establish residue-specific resonance assignments and characterize its conformational properties in an aqueous solution. Backbone and side-chain resonances were assigned using multidimensional NMR spectroscopy, including 1H-15N HMQC, TOCSY, and NOESY experiments. Reliable sequential NOE connectivities were identified for several peptide segments, while ambiguous and unresolved resonances were conservatively excluded from the structural interpretation. The N-terminal Aib2 residue served as an important assignment anchor but did not define a stable terminal structure. In contrast, the Aib13 region exhibited a locally organized backbone environment with a short helical-like conformational tendency, suggesting Aib13-centered local ordering within the peptide chain. Structure calculations based on the 1.2 GHz NMR and CD experiments revealed that tirzepatide does not adopt a single rigid conformation in solution but instead exists as a conformational ensemble composed of locally ordered and flexible regions. These findings provide a residue-specific view of tirzepatide dynamics in solution and offer structural insights into the conformational landscape of this therapeutically important peptide.

title: Retatrutide Once Weekly in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis Pain and Obesity.
journal: The New England journal of medicine
abstract: Retatrutide, an investigational triple agonist of GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors, may be useful for the treatment of painful knee osteoarthritis in persons with obesity. In two phase 3 trials, adults without diabetes who had painful knee osteoarthritis and a body-mass index of at least 27 were randomly assigned to receive once-weekly subcutaneous retatrutide (9 or 12 mg in TRIUMPH-4 and 4, 9, or 12 mg in TRIUMPH-1-OA) or placebo. In TRIUMPH-4, the primary end points were the change in the WOMAC pain score (range, 0 to 10, with higher scores indicating worse pain) and the percent change in body weight at week 68. In TRIUMPH-1-OA, the primary end point was the change in the WOMAC pain score at week 80. For non-pain-related end points, intercurrent events were handled with a treatment-policy strategy. For pain-related end points, a hybrid-treatment estimand was applied, with a hypothetical strategy for intercurrent events that suggested treatment failure and a treatment-policy strategy elsewhere. We also report results for an intention-to-treat (ITT) estimand. A total of 445 participants underwent randomization in TRIUMPH-4 and 574 in TRIUMPH-1-OA. At 68 weeks, the mean changes in the WOMAC pain score (hybrid-treatment estimand) with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-4 were -3.96 (9 mg) and -3.74 (12 mg), versus -2.12 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -1.83 [95% confidence interval {CI}, -2.37 to -1.30] and -1.61 [95% CI, -2.16 to -1.07], respectively). For the ITT estimand, the corresponding differences from placebo were -1.70 (95% CI, -2.19 to -1.22) and -1.38 (95% CI, -1.91 to -0.85) (P<0.001 for all comparisons). The mean percent changes in body weight with retatrutide were -20.0% (9 mg) and -23.7% (12 mg), versus -4.6% with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -15.4 percentage points [95% CI, -18.7 to -12.1] and -19.2 percentage points [95% CI, -22.4 to -15.9]; P<0.001 for both comparisons). At 80 weeks, the mean changes in the WOMAC pain score (hybrid-treatment estimand) with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-1-OA were -3.22 (4 mg), -3.48 (9 mg), and -3.64 (12 mg), versus -1.87 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -1.35 [95% CI, -1.92 to -0.78], -1.61 [95% CI, -2.20 to -1.02], and -1.77 [95% CI, -2.34 to -1.20], respectively). For the ITT estimand, the corresponding differences from placebo were -0.96 (95% CI, -1.61 to -0.30), -1.41 (95% CI, -2.07 to -0.75), and -1.64 (95% CI, -2.26 to -1.02) (P≤0.005 for all comparisons). In both trials, serious adverse events were more common with retatrutide than with placebo, and the most common adverse events were gastrointestinal. In participants with painful knee osteoarthritis and obesity, treatment with retatrutide resulted in significantly greater reductions in both the WOMAC pain score and body weight than placebo. (Funded by Eli Lilly; TRIUMPH-4 and -1 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT05931367 and NCT05929066.).

title: Longitudinal Taxonomic and Predicted Functional Gut Microbiome Responses to Tirzepatide and Semaglutide: An Exploratory Secondary Analysis of the OMDOT-1 Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1-based therapies improve metabolic outcomes, but longitudinal gut microbiome dynamics remain poorly characterized. We compared taxonomic and predicted functional microbiome responses to tirzepatide and semaglutide in Type 2 diabetes. This exploratory secondary analysis included 36 participants from a randomized controlled trial comparing tirzepatide, semaglutide and conventional treatment. Faecal samples were collected at five time points over 16 weeks and analyzed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Genus-level features were screened using MaAsLin2, and candidate genera were further evaluated using longitudinal mixed-effects models. Predicted microbial functions were inferred using PICRUSt2 and analyzed using MaAsLin2. Primary analyses were adjusted for baseline body mass index, with exploratory sensitivity analyses additionally adjusted for changes in body weight and haemoglobin A1c. No significant between-group differences in beta diversity were observed. Alpha diversity increased predominantly in the tirzepatide group, with a significant time-by-treatment interaction versus control. Longitudinal trajectories relative to the control group differed for several genera, including Romboutsia_B, Barnesiella and Ruminococcus_E with both treatments and Vescimonas with tirzepatide (q < 0.05). Across 2106 predicted EC features, longitudinal effects were positively correlated between tirzepatide and semaglutide (67.1% concordant direction; Pearson r = 0.450, p < 0.001). Treatment-versus-control analyses identified predicted functional changes involving energy and carbohydrate metabolism. Tirzepatide and semaglutide were associated with partially distinct taxonomic changes, accompanied by broadly similar predicted functional patterns. These longitudinal findings complement, while remaining distinct from, Week-16 shotgun metagenomic endpoint analyses. Japan Registry of Clinical Trials (jRCT), jRCT1051240017.

title: Lean Body Mass During GLP-1-Based Therapy and the Potential Role of Dietary Protein: Evidence From Energy-Restriction Trials.
Weaker or Just Lighter? Monitoring Strength and Function, Not Just Lean Mass, During GLP-1 Weight Loss.
abstract: Body-composition studies of GLP-1-based therapy report how much of the weight lost is lean mass, not whether the patient is getting weaker. This review asks how to monitor strength and function during treatment. Narrative review of October 2026 PubMed searches pairing incretin drugs with strength, performance, walking and measurement-error terms, plus hand-checked reference lists. In older adults, strength declines about three times faster than lean mass and predicts mortality where lean mass does not. On GLP-1-based therapy, randomized trials show longer walks and better reported function, while some cohorts of older adults show falling strength and gait speed; a 2026 review of 35 body-composition trials found none that measured objective physical function. Recent recommendations advise assessing strength and function, but none identified here judges change against measurement error. Functional discordance is a confirmed within-person decline in strength or physical performance beyond measurement error without an adverse lean-mass signal (exploratory default: lean loss beyond the scan's least significant change and above 40% of weight lost). For higher-risk patients (older adults; low strength, frailty or rapid weight loss), the review proposes grip strength, five-times chair-stand time and usual gait speed, with a timed stair climb where feasible, before treatment, at 3, 6 and 12 months and around dose changes, with declines confirmed by repeat testing, assistance recorded and stepwise clinical review. The schedule is pragmatic and not validated. If lean-mass change identifies the patients whose function declines, functional monitoring may add little; if discordance is common, lean mass is an inadequate surrogate.

title: Effects of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists on Hyperuricemia, Serum Uric Acid and Gout: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Hyperuricemia and gout are common but underappreciated comorbidities in Type 2 diabetes (T2D), obesity and chronic kidney disease (CKD). We aimed to quantify the pooled effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1 receptor agonists on serum uric acid (SUA), incident gout and hyperuricemia, and to determine whether these effects vary by drug class and are mediated by weight loss. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL and ClinicalTrials.gov through July 2026 for RCTs of ≥ 12 weeks' duration reporting SUA change, gout flares or hyperuricemia incidence. Random-effects meta-analysis, subgroup and sensitivity analyses and meta-regression were performed. Registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261468511). Eighteen RCTs (77 942 participants) met inclusion criteria. Incretin-based therapy significantly reduced SUA versus control (weighted mean difference [WMD] -0.44 mg/dL, 95% CI -0.52 to -0.35), reduced incident gout flares (hazard ratio [HR] 0.62, 95% CI 0.53-0.72), and reduced hyperuricemia incidence (odds ratio [OR] 0.61, 95% CI 0.53-0.70). Dual GIP/GLP-1 RA (tirzepatide) produced greater SUA lowering than mono GLP-1 RAs (-0.62 vs. -0.35 mg/dL, p = 0.001). Body-weight loss was a significant moderator of SUA reduction (β = -0.041 mg/dL per kg, p < 0.001), explaining 84.7% of between-trial heterogeneity, with a significant weight-independent intercept (-0.19 mg/dL, p < 0.001). The SUA reduction was robust in all sensitivity analyses, including restriction to placebo-controlled trials. GRADE certainty was high for SUA and moderate for gout flares (owing to small-study effects) and hyperuricemia incidence. Incretin-based therapies were associated with modest reductions in SUA and with a lower incidence of gout flares and hyperuricemia, an effect largely related to weight loss. The clinical relevance of these effects, and the mechanism of any weight-independent component, remains uncertain and warrant confirmation in dedicated trials.

title: Medicaid Coverage Withdrawal and Dispensing of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists for Obesity.
abstract: Five state Medicaid programs withdrew coverage of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) for obesity in late 2025 and January 2026, and others have narrowed coverage or are reconsidering it. The benefits of these drugs appear to depend on continued use, but whether withdrawal interrupts treatment for current users is unknown. This study examined changes in dispensing of obesity-indicated GLP-1 RAs after state Medicaid programs withdrew or restricted coverage. This quasi-experimental study used quarterly Medicaid State Drug Utilization Data for 50 states and the District of Columbia from 2021 through the first quarter of 2026. Difference-in-differences and event-study models compared dispensing in states that withdrew coverage with dispensing in states that continued it, using each state's dispensing of diabetes-indicated GLP-1 RAs as a within-state comparison. The exposure was withdrawal or restriction of Medicaid coverage of GLP-1 RAs for obesity, identified from state agency documents. The main outcome was reimbursed prescriptions for obesity-indicated GLP-1 RAs per 1,000 enrollees per quarter. Estimates are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Data were analyzed from September to October 2026. The five withdrawing states accounted for 2,428,709 (65.2%) of 3,725,732 obesity-indicated GLP-1 RA prescriptions reimbursed by Medicaid in 2025. Compared with 12 continuing states, withdrawal was associated with an 84.7% decline in obesity-indicated dispensing (95% CI: 64.5%-93.4%; exact permutation p < 0.001), or 29.1 fewer prescriptions per 1,000 enrollees per quarter (95% CI: 14.3-43.9). No significant change was detected in diabetes-indicated dispensing (-3.2%; 95% CI: -23.4% to 22.2%), and differences between the two groups before the withdrawals were announced were small and not statistically significant. In the first quarter without coverage, obesity-indicated dispensing fell by 61% to 96% in individual withdrawing states. The four states that withdrew on January 1, 2026, reimbursed 661,353 obesity-indicated prescriptions in the preceding quarter and 134,647 in the next, a decline of 526,706 (79.6%). Dispensing of older antiobesity medications increased by at most 2.9 prescriptions per 1,000 enrollees. Narrower criteria in two states were followed by declines of 23%-37%. In this quasi-experimental study, withdrawal of Medicaid coverage was associated with the loss of most reimbursed dispensing of GLP-1 RAs for obesity within one quarter, with little replacement by other agents. Protecting enrollees already receiving these drugs, for example, by honoring existing authorizations, might limit treatment interruption, but this has not been evaluated.

title: Psychiatric symptoms, psychological well-being and quality of life after metabolic and bariatric surgery versus incretin-based therapy in obesity: The role of weight loss.
abstract: Metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) and incretin-based pharmacotherapy (GLP-1 receptor agonists) cause substantial weight loss, but whether the accompanying psychological improvement is associated with the degree of weight loss or with treatment-specific mechanisms is unclear. To compare changes in psychiatric symptoms, psychological well-being and quality of life after MBS and incretin-based therapy, and to examine the role of weight loss. In this prospective, non-randomized cohort study, 207 adults with obesity (MBS, n = 97; incretin-based pharmacotherapy, n = 110 [tirzepatide 87, semaglutide 19, liraglutide 4]) completed 16 psychiatric and quality-of-life scales before treatment and at 6 months. Weight loss was 33.2 ± 9.9 kg with MBS and 16.8 ± 11.5 kg with pharmacotherapy. Both groups improved significantly on all 16 scales (r = 0.28-0.84; all p ≤ 0.02). With pharmacotherapy, improvement correlated with weight loss on all scales (all p ≤ 0.04; |r| = 0.20-0.45); after MBS, no association was observed (all p > 0.5). Crude between-group differences favoring MBS (5/16 scales) disappeared after adjustment for weight loss. Only emotion regulation difficulties showed a significant group × time interaction (coefficient 3.3, 95% CI 0.7-5.9). Both groups showed improved psychological well-being and quality of life. Improvement tracked weight loss with pharmacotherapy but not after MBS, possibly reflecting less variable weight loss after surgery. The crude advantage of MBS was no longer evident after adjusting for weight loss, suggesting an association with greater weight loss rather than a modality-specific effect, with emotion regulation as a possible exception.

title: Clinical pharmacology of antidiabetic drugs: an update.
abstract: This review describes the updated pharmacology of antidiabetic drugs and its translation into clinical applications. English language literature published from January 1, 1998 to July 25, 2026 was collected using PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Ovid. Research articles, reviews, and clinical practice guidelines were included for discussion. Currently, ultra-long-acting basal insulins are emerging, allowing less frequent injections. Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), tirzepatide, and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) have novel pharmacodynamic properties and clinical evidence of cardiorenal and metabolic benefits, supporting their important roles in individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2D) who have high cardiorenal risk. Because of their effects on weight reduction, GLP-1RAs (semaglutide, liraglutide, and orforglipron) and tirzepatide are approved for the treatment of obesity. Furthermore, SGLT2is (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and sotagliflozin) provide cardiorenal benefits, with supporting potential mechanisms, in individuals with heart failure and chronic kidney disease. Conventional oral drugs (e.g., metformin, thiazolidinediones, dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors, sulfonylureas, meglitinides, and α-glucosidase inhibitors) lack sufficient pharmacologic and clinical data on cardiorenal benefits, suggesting their roles as adjunctive therapies. Novel candidates, including triple incretin hormone agonists (acting on GLP-1, glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide [GIP], and glucagon receptors), GLP-1RA-GIP antagonism-based therapies, amylin analogues, and new dual SGLT1/2 inhibitors, show promising results for glycemic control and weight loss. Overall, a comprehensive understanding of the pharmacologic characteristics of antidiabetic drugs promotes appropriate drug use for the management of T2D and cardiometabolic diseases and helps avoid undesirable events. Ongoing investigations of novel approaches may contribute to improved patient care in the future.

title: Rethinking endpoints for anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in patients with HR+ early breast cancer receiving endocrine therapy: from body weight and BMI to body composition.
abstract: Body weight (BW) and body mass index (BMI) are commonly used to assess obesity and response to weight-management interventions in patients with hormone receptor-positive (HR+) early breast cancer (eBC) receiving endocrine therapy. However, these measures do not adequately reflect changes in fat mass, visceral adiposity, lean mass and sarcopenia-related phenotypes. This focused narrative review examines whether BW and BMI are sufficient endpoints for evaluating obesity management and anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in patients with HR+ eBC receiving endocrine therapy. PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched for relevant evidence until 23 June 2026, including BC-specific studies of obesity pharmacotherapy and registered interventional trials. Studies have reported increases in total and visceral fat mass after adjuvant BC treatment, while changes in lean mass have been less consistent. The identified BC-specific studies remain mainly retrospective and weight-centric, with none assessing body composition as a key outcome. BW and BMI may be useful entry and monitoring variables, but insufficient as stand-alone endpoints. Body composition should be considered as a complementary endpoint, alongside metabolic, functional and oncologic outcomes. Future studies should also assess endocrine therapy adherence and persistence to better characterize the benefits and risks of anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in patients with HR+ eBC.

title: Persistence and geographic availability of Medicare Part D coverage for non-diabetes GLP-1 therapies, 2024-2026.
Antidiabetic Therapy and Atrial Fibrillation: Pathophysiological Links, Therapeutic Implications, and Evidence-Based Outcomes.
abstract: Diabetes Mellitus (DM) is strongly associated with an increased risk, severity, and recurrence of Atrial Fibrillation (AF). This narrative review aims to synthesize the mechanistic links between DM and AF and evaluate the impact of major antidiabetic drug categories on AF incidence, burden, and post-ablation outcomes. A focused narrative review of the literature was conducted using predefined eligibility criteria for study selection and specific keywords to search major scientific databases and grey literature. Hyperglycemia, oxidative stress, epicardial adipose tissue expansion, autonomic imbalance, and atrial remodeling represent core pathophysiological mechanisms connecting DM and AF. Among antidiabetic pharmacotherapies, the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist semaglutide displays a potential to reduce AF incidence. Sodium-glucose transporter 2 inhibitors have similarly been shown to lower the incidence of AF in most of the available evidence, while offering an emerging, preliminary benefit for post-ablation success. Metformin also demonstrates a positive impact across both primary and secondary AF prevention, albeit with less robust evidence. Other incretin therapies, including tirzepatide, exhibit neutral effects, while thiazolidinediones and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors yield conflicting results. Data from insulin and sulfonylureas suggest an unfavorable risk profile, though potentially confounded by indication. Antidiabetic therapy selection may have clinically meaningful implications for AF risk modification and rhythm-control outcomes. Weight-centric and cardio-protective strategies, particularly SGLT2 inhibitors and semaglutide, alongside the traditional option of metformin, show promising signals. Nevertheless, available data derive largely from unadjudicated adverseevent reporting and observational cohorts, currently precluding definitive class-wide or agentspecific recommendations. Incorporating atrial fibrillation risk into the individualization of antidiabetic therapy is a promising and clinically relevant strategy. However, establishing any specific agent as a preferred option for AF management remains premature in the absence of dedicated trials with primary AF endpoints.

title: Tirzepatide for the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea: from apnea-hypopnea index reduction to cardiometabolic risk mitigation-a narrative review.
abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a chronic respiratory disorder with nocturnal oxygen desaturation that is often associated with multisystemic sequelae such as hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, and increased morbidity and mortality. Obesity has been proposed as a modifiable risk factor; hence, the recent shift in focus to investigating anti-obesity medications for the management of OSA. Tirzepatide is the first U.S. FDA-approved pharmacotherapy for the treatment of moderate-to-severe OSA in adults with obesity to be utilized in combination with low caloric intake and physical activity, given its prior success in managing type 2 diabetes (T2D) and obesity. This narrative review evaluates tirzepatide and the SURMOUNT-OSA trial program as the key contemporary anchors for the pharmacological treatment of OSA in adults with concurrent obesity. Because the randomized evidence base currently comprises a single pivotal trial program, the review centers on SURMOUNT-OSA and its prespecified endpoints along with post hoc analyses, supplemented by observational, modeling, and mechanistic studies. In the SURMOUNT-OSA program, tirzepatide produced randomized, placebo-controlled reductions in the apnea-hypopnea index, sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden, body weight, and systemic inflammation. The program was designed around respiratory and metabolic endpoints rather than clinical events, so it cannot support conclusions about mortality, cardiovascular, or renal outcomes. Favorable signals for those events, including all-cause mortality, major adverse kidney events, and major adverse cardiovascular events, come only from nonrandomized observational cohorts and are best regarded as directional and exploratory rather than definitive. Tirzepatide may help frame OSA as a multifactorial and partially metabolically treatable disease and may represent a clinically meaningful expansion of treatment options alongside, rather than as a replacement for, established mechanical and procedural therapies. The available evidence is anchored in a single phase 3 trial program and limited by short follow-up and the absence of definitive comparative and long-term outcome data. Long-term durability of effect after discontinuation, generalizability beyond the SURMOUNT-OSA-eligible population, OSA-specific economic analysis, and head-to-head comparisons against CPAP remain the principal unsettled questions requiring dedicated long-term studies before firm clinical recommendations can be made.

title: [New oral anti-obesity drugs: the future or second choice?].
abstract: Obesity and its comorbidities represent a growing worldwide health challenge. To date, lifestyle modification is the most frequently used treatment modality, but offers only limited success in terms of both the extent and maintenance of weight loss. Potent injectable incretin mimetics such as semaglutide and tirzepatide were recently introduced as novel pharmacological options for improved and clinically meaningful weight management. In 2026, the first two oral glucagon-like peptide‑1 (GLP-1)-based agents, namely oral semaglutide and orforglipron, were approved and are promoted as alternative drug choices for additional weight loss, allowing people with obesity to make their own choice from a broader spectrum of therapeutics. This review describes the current state of knowledge on these new medications for the treatment of obesity. A variety of other oral drugs is currently under development and will substantially expand obesity management in the coming years.

title: Semaglutide, Tirzepatide and Clinically Recorded Alcohol-Related Outcomes in Type 2 Diabetes: A Target Trial Emulation.
abstract: To compare the risk of incident alcohol use disorder (AUD) among adults with Type 2 diabetes (T2D) initiating semaglutide, tirzepatide or sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i). We conducted a target trial emulation using de-identified electronic health record data from the TriNetX research network (June 2022-January 2025). Adults with T2D newly initiating semaglutide, tirzepatide or an SGLT2i were included. The primary outcome was clinically recorded hospitalization or emergency department (ED) visits for AUD. Cox proportional hazards models with 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM) estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs. Sensitivity and subgroup analyses as well as secondary outcomes assessed the robustness of the findings. During a mean follow-up of 0.81-1.02 years, the incidence rates (IRs) of clinically recorded hospitalization or ED visits for AUD were 2.42 versus 4.53 per 1000 person-years for semaglutide versus SGLT2i, with an HR of 0.54 (95% CI, 0.45-0.64). Similarly, the IRs were 2.34 versus 3.98 per 1000 person-years for tirzepatide versus SGLT2i, with an HR of 0.61 (95% CI, 0.46-0.83). In the direct comparison of semaglutide versus tirzepatide, IRs were 2.43 and 2.36 per 1000 person-years, respectively, with no difference in risk (HR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.73-1.31). Results were consistent across sensitivity and subgroup analyses and secondary outcomes. In adults with T2D, semaglutide and tirzepatide were associated with lower rates of clinically recorded AUD-related outcomes than SGLT2i, with no difference between the two GLP-1RA medications.

title: Discovery, optimization, and phase 1 evaluation of a novel, orally available GLP-1R/GIPR dual agonist.
abstract: The efficacy and convenience of anti-diabetic and anti-obesity therapeutics have surged in recent years due to the emergence of incretin-based poly-pharmacological approaches as well as advances in the oral delivery of peptide drugs. We sought to combine both strategies in an orally deliverable dual agonist of the GLP-1 and GIP receptors. We designed a panel of unimolecular, fatty-acylated peptide dual agonists, which was screened for receptor potencies in cell-based assay systems. NNC0130 was selected to advance into clinical studies using both oral and subcutaneous administration. NNC0130 exhibited in vitro potency comparable to semaglutide at human GLP-1R and to tirzepatide at human GIPR, with a chemical structure compatible with semi-recombinant production. Its human half-life of 76-89 h was deemed suitable for once-daily oral administration. In a multiple-ascending dose trial in participants with overweight or obesity and with separate subcutaneous and oral cohorts, daily subcutaneous administration of NNC0130 escalating from 0.3 to 3.0 mg per dose provided a placebo-corrected mean body weight loss of 9% after 12 weeks of treatment and 12% after 15 weeks. Daily oral administration escalating from 5 to 50 mg per dose provided a placebo-corrected mean body weight loss of 4% after 12 weeks, which was not statistically significantly different from zero. The relative oral bioavailability when co-formulated with permeation enhancer salcaprozate sodium was estimated to 1.6-2.2% versus s. c. administration. The modest weight lowering efficacy of orally administered NNC0130 highlights the continued challenges of low oral bioavailability of acylated peptides. However, the substantial efficacy observed with subcutaneous administration motivated advancement into Phase 2 clinical development.

title: Digital Augmentation of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 for Obesity Management: Retrospective Study.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), including semaglutide and tirzepatide, are highly effective for weight management; however, long-term outcomes depend on sustained behavioral engagement. Digital health tools may enhance these behavioral components, but evidence regarding their real-world benefit alongside pharmacotherapy remains limited. This study aims to evaluate whether augmenting a direct-to-consumer GLP-1 RA program with a behavioral support smartphone app improves weight-loss outcomes compared with medication alone, and to identify which app features are associated with weight loss over time. A retrospective observational cohort study was conducted using data from 6113 adults (older than 18 years) in Australia who self-enrolled into the Mosh direct-to-consumer weight-loss program between July 1, 2024, and August 13, 2025, with their weight data recorded at baseline and at least 1 other timepoint. Participants received semaglutide or tirzepatide, with optional access to a smartphone app and clinician support. Logistic regression models examined achievement of ≥5%, ≥10%, and ≥15% weight-loss thresholds at 60, 120, and 180 days. Linear mixed-effects models interacting with app feature use, with linear and quadratic time terms, assessed the association of different features with percentage weight loss trajectories over time. Both models adjusted for medication type, gender, ethnicity, age, and baseline BMI. Participants using the program plus medication had higher odds of achieving clinically significant weight loss than those using medication only. Adjusted odds ratio point estimates for day 60, 120, and 180 (±10) days indicated they were 1.38 (95% CI 1.09-1.75) times to 2.22 (95% CI 1.40-3.45) times more likely to achieve ≥5% weight loss across timepoints, 1.67 (95% CI 1.33-2.10) times to 1.97 (95% CI 1.35-2.90) times more likely to achieve ≥10% weight loss by day 120 and 180, and 1.99 (95% CI 1.26-3.29) times more likely to achieve ≥15% weight loss by 180 days. Mixed-effects modeling demonstrated that progress logging was associated with more rapid weight loss over time (β=.26 percentage-point additional weight lost per 30 days, SE 0.06; t4336=4.46; 95% CI 0.14-0.38; P<.001). No other app features were consistently associated with changes in weight-loss trajectories. Augmenting GLP-1 RA treatment with a behavioral smartphone app was associated with a higher likelihood of achieving clinically significant weight loss, although differences in overall weight-loss trajectories were modest. Progress logging emerged as the primary behavioral predictor of improved outcomes. While not causal effects, these findings are consistent with the positive value of integrating digital tools with pharmacotherapy for weight loss.

title: Cardiometabolic benefits of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and dual agonists: from obesity and diabetes to heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.
abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) accounts for over half of all heart failure hospitalisations and is increasing in prevalence, largely driven by obesity and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM). Glucagon-like-peptide receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and the dual GLP-1/GIP agonist, tirzepatide, have been shown to be safe and effective medications in the treatment of T2DM and obesity as well as in obesity-related HFpEF. This review summarises the pathophysiology of obesity-related HFpEF, mechanisms by which GLP-1 RAs and tirzepatide may improve symptoms and outcomes, and summarise evidence from recent randomised controlled and observational trials across the disease spectrum they have been studied in. Therapeutic implications and future research directions are also discussed. A structured literature search was performed using PubMed/MEDLINE and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) up to August 2025. GLP-1 receptor agonists and tirzepatide represent a promising therapeutic advance for obesity-related HFpEF. Benefits are likely mediated through weight loss dependent and weight-loss independent mechanisms. Important uncertainties remain regarding their role in non-obese HFpEF, optimal patient selection, and their safety in HFrEF.

title: Management of Obesity in Special Populations and Limited-Resource Settings: An Egyptian Medical Position Statement.
journal: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy
abstract: Obesity/adiposity-based chronic disease is a chronic progressive relapsing disease linked to several comorbidities, with rising prevalence in Egypt. Limited local guidelines and healthcare challenges necessitate evidence-based, culturally adapted strategies. The Egyptian Medical Association for the Study of Obesity convened a clinical multidisciplinary panel to develop consensus recommendations. Evidence was synthesized from literature, prioritizing resource-limited settings and special situations. Assessment: Move beyond Body Mass Index to include waist circumference, waist/height ratio, body composition, and screening for obesity-related complications and diseases. Lifestyle Interventions: a-Nutrition: Mediterranean/dietary approach to stop hypertension diets, slow eating, and supervised fasting (eg Ramadan and Christian). b-Activity: Culturally tailored approaches (eg prayer-time movement and Arabic apps). c-Behavior: Cognitive-behavioral therapy and family-inclusive support. Pharmacotherapy: Use of approved agents (orlistat, naltrexone/bupropion, liraglutide, semaglutide, and tirzepatide) according to obesity-related complications and diseases and age group. Avoid GLP-1, GLP-1/GIP analogues in patients with medullary thyroid cancer, and all agents during pregnancy. Bariatric Surgery: Indicated for body mass index ≥40 kg/m2 (or ≥35 with obesity-related complications and diseases), with lifelong micronutrient supplementation. Special Populations: a-Adolescents: Focus on growth, not only weight-loss; consider pharmacotherapy in different age groups. b-Elderly: Prioritize muscle preservation; avoid weight loss unless obesity-related complications and diseases exist. c-Pregnancy: No weight loss; delay postpartum interventions until lactation is established. Policy Actions: Mandate food labeling, tax sugar-sweetened beverages, and integrate obesity services into primary healthcare. These recommendations provide a pragmatic framework for obesity/adiposity-based chronic disease management in Egypt, emphasizing affordable, patient-centered care, and clinical multidisciplinary collaboration and policy support.

title: Semaglutide or Tirzepatide Added to Psychological Support in Binge Eating Disorder With Overweight or Obesity: The LEAP-BED Prospective Pilot Study.
Bariatric Surgery as a Rescue Strategy After Semaglutide or Tirzepatide.
abstract: To evaluate 2-year weight loss after bariatric surgery among adults with intolerable adverse effects or inadequate weight loss with semaglutide or tirzepatide. Semaglutide and tirzepatide are effective obesity medications, but intolerance and inadequate weight loss are common, creating uncertainty about next-step therapy. This retrospective cohort included adults with BMI ≥35 kg/m² undergoing Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) or sleeve gastrectomy (SG) at Cleveland Clinic hospitals from 2018 to 2024. Electronic health record and dispensing data classified preoperative semaglutide or tirzepatide exposure and response. The primary outcome was estimated 2-year total body weight loss (TBWL), stratified by procedure and type 2 diabetes (T2DM) status. Among 4929 patients, 4661 had no prior exposure (comparator group), 61 discontinued semaglutide or tirzepatide because of intolerable adverse effects, and 207 had inadequate weight-loss response. Before surgery, estimated 2-year medication-associated weight change was a 1.4% gain in the intolerance group and 1.5% TBWL in the inadequate-response group. After surgery, 2-year TBWL in the intolerance group was 27.9% and 22.7% after RYGB and 20.1% and 21.6% after SG among patients without and with T2DM, respectively. Corresponding estimates in the inadequate-response group were 35.8%, 27.4%, 14.3%, and 14.2%. For comparison, corresponding 2-year TBWL estimates in the comparator group were 33.3%, 28.7%, 23.6%, and 19.9%. In adjusted analysis of the inadequate-response group, RYGB was associated with greater 2-year TBWL than SG (32.7% vs. 17.8%; difference, 14.9 percentage points [95% CI, 13.1%-16.7%]). Bariatric surgery was associated with clinically meaningful 2-year weight loss after semaglutide or tirzepatide intolerance or inadequate response, with RYGB potentially offering greater benefit after inadequate response.

title: The effect of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists on bone metabolism: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials of predominantly first-generation agents.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) improve cardiometabolic outcomes, but their isolated effects on human bone remodeling remain uncertain because prior syntheses pooled heterogeneous study designs and active antidiabetic comparators. This systematic review and meta-analysis quantified the effects of GLP-1RAs versus placebo on densitometric, biochemical, and inflammatory markers of bone metabolism in randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and PubMed/MEDLINE were searched from inception through May 12, 2026 for randomized placebo-controlled trials of GLP-1RAs or dual incretin agonists administered for 12 to 52 weeks. Eleven trials provided compatible data for random-effects meta-analysis and one additional trial was synthesized narratively, comprising 11 trials of first-generation agents (exenatide, dulaglutide, liraglutide) and one trial of second-generation semaglutide (1.0 mg/week), with zero eligible placebo-controlled trials identified for semaglutide 2.4 mg/week or tirzepatide. Weighted mean differences (WMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) bone mineral density (BMD), bone turnover markers, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), and evidence certainty was rated using GRADE. Compared with placebo, GLP-1RA treatment reduced lumbar spine BMD (WMD: -0.02 g/cm2, 95% CI: -0.03 to -0.00, I2 = 0.0%; 3 trials, N = 222; Moderate certainty) and increased the bone resorption marker C-terminal telopeptide (CTX) (WMD: 0.05 μg/L, 95% CI: 0.01 to 0.08, I2 = 72.5%; 6 trials, N = 439; Low certainty), while reducing serum hs-CRP (WMD: -0.49 mg/L, 95% CI: -0.97 to -0.00, I2 = 0.0%; 4 trials [5 arms], N = 340; Low certainty). No significant differences were observed for femoral neck BMD (WMD: 0.01 g/cm2, 95% CI: -0.02 to 0.04, I2 = 68.9%; 5 trials [6 arms], N = 323; Very Low certainty), total hip BMD (WMD: 0.00 g/cm2, 95% CI: -0.02 to 0.03, I2 = 70.8%; 5 trials [6 arms], N = 382; Low certainty), or procollagen type 1 N-terminal propeptide (P1NP) (WMD: -1.24 μg/L, 95% CI: -3.61 to 1.13, I2 = 0.0%; 5 trials, N = 399; Moderate certainty), and leave-one-out exclusion of the single semaglutide trial did not alter the direction or significance of any pooled estimate. Treatment with predominantly first-generation GLP-1RAs over 12 to 52 weeks increases osteoclastic bone resorption and induces a small, borderline reduction in lumbar spine BMD while preserving hip BMD and lowering systemic inflammation. Because existing placebo-controlled RCTs largely reflect earlier-generation agents with moderate weight loss, these findings cannot be extrapolated to higher-potency anti-obesity therapies such as semaglutide 2.4 mg/week or tirzepatide, which require dedicated long-term skeletal safety trials.

title: Tirzepatide-associated severe euvolemic hyponatremia with syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion-compatible biochemical features.
abstract: Tirzepatide is a dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist that is being increasingly used for the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity. Gastrointestinal adverse effects associated with incretin-based therapies can influence water balance through nonosmotic vasopressin release and reduced oral solute intake. In this case report, we report a patient who developed severe symptomatic hyponatremia with biochemical features compatible with the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion temporally associated with tirzepatide therapy. A woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus and morbid obesity on regular insulin and chronic torsemide therapy presented with anorexia, weakness, and drowsiness 10 days after tirzepatide administration. Serum sodium was 104 mmol/L, and she was clinically euvolemic. Renal, hepatic, hematologic, acid-base, and other endocrine parameters were normal. The calculated serum osmolality was 224 mOsm/kg. Urinary sodium remained elevated after withdrawal of the diuretic. The patient was managed with fluid restriction and hypertonic saline, and this resulted in progressive correction of sodium and clinical improvement. This case suggests a potential association between tirzepatide therapy and severe euvolemic hyponatremia. Clinicians should consider electrolyte monitoring in patients receiving incretin-based therapy who develop significant gastrointestinal symptoms or reduced oral intake.

title: PET Imaging of Dual GLP-1R and GIPR Targeting with [18F]AlF-NOTA-Asp2-Tirzepatide.
abstract: Tirzepatide is a clinical dual GLP-1R and GIPR agonist for type 2 diabetes and obesity, and non-invasive approaches to assess its in vivo biodistribution and systemic toxicity in living animals remain limited. Both receptors also serve as potential targets for neuroendocrine tumor imaging, and dual-target PET probes for simultaneous GLP-1R and GIPR detection are still lacking. Herein, we developed a novel PET probe [18F]AlF-NOTA-Asp2-tirzepatide via structural modification of tirzepatide. This probe successfully visualized the in vivo distribution of tirzepatide, which was primarily eliminated through the renal system. The C20 fatty diacid moiety caused elevated uptake in the heart, liver and blood due to enhanced albumin binding. In vitro assays verified its reliable GLP-1R and moderate GIPR binding affinity. Persistent tumor accumulation was observed in INS-1 and A549-GIPR xenografts, allowing effective tumor visualization. In summary, [18F]AlF-NOTA-Asp2-tirzepatide features facile radiolabeling and enables the clear visualization of tirzepatide in vivo, along with favorable dual-targeting performance, while excessive non-target uptake still needs to be optimized for further clinical translation.

title: Efficacy and safety of oral orforglipron in Japanese participants with obesity disease (ATTAIN-J): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, phase 3 trial.
abstract: Orforglipron, a small-molecule, non-peptide, oral GLP-1 receptor agonist, has shown bodyweight reduction and cardiometabolic benefits in adults with obesity across phase 3 trials globally. We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of orforglipron versus placebo for treating obesity disease in Japanese adults. ATTAIN-J was a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, phase 3 trial conducted across 16 medical research centres and hospitals in Japan and included adults aged 18 years or older with a BMI between 27 kg/m2 and less than 35 kg/m2 and two or more obesity-related health disorders, or a BMI of 35 kg/m2 or higher and one or more obesity-related health disorder, with one or more of the obesity-related health disorders being hypertension, dyslipidaemia, or type 2 diabetes (targeted at about 25% of participants), consistent with Japanese indications for tirzepatide and semaglutide for obesity disease; and at least one unsuccessful dietary attempt to lose weight. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) via a computer-generated sequence to once-daily oral orforglipron (6 mg, 12 mg, or 36 mg) or placebo. Co-primary endpoints were mean percentage change in bodyweight and percentage of participants with at least 5% bodyweight reduction from baseline to week 72. Efficacy endpoints were primarily evaluated by the treatment regimen estimand in all randomly assigned participants. Safety was assessed in participants who received at least one dose of study treatment. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05931380 (completed). Between July 31, 2023, and June 19, 2025, 291 participants were screened, of whom 238 (144 [61%] males and 94 [39%] females; mean age 54·1 years [SD 11·2]) were randomly assigned to receive orforglipron 6 mg (n=61), 12 mg (n=57), or 36 mg (n=60), or placebo (n=60); 214 (90%) participants completed the study. At week 72, mean percentage change in bodyweight was -5·9% (95% CI -7·6 to -4·2) with orforglipron 6 mg, -8·7% (-10·9 to -6·5) with 12 mg, and -7·9% (-10·0 to -5·8) with 36 mg, compared with -0·6% (-2·1 to 0·8) with placebo (all p<0·0001 vs placebo). At week 72, a bodyweight reduction of at least 5% was seen in 15·2% (SE 4·8; nine of 60) of participants in the placebo group compared with 45·6% (6·1; 28 of 61; p=0·0001) of participants in the orforglipron 6 mg group, 60·8% (6·4; 35 of 57; p<0·0001) of participants in the orforglipron 12 mg group, and 58·8% (6·5; 35 of 60; p<0·0001) of participants in the orforglipron 36 mg group. Adverse events with orforglipron were mostly mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal symptoms. Across all orforglipron groups, treatment-emergent adverse events that most frequently led to study treatment discontinuation were nausea (one [2%] of 61 in the 6 mg group, one [2%] of 57 in the 12 mg group, and five [8%] of 60 in the 36 mg group vs none with placebo) and vomiting (none in the 6 mg group, two [4%] in the 12 mg group, and one [2%] in the 36 mg group vs none in the placebo group). In Japanese adults with obesity disease, once-daily orforglipron resulted in statistically superior reductions in bodyweight versus placebo, with a safety profile consistent with that of other GLP-1 receptor agonists. Eli Lilly and Company. For the Japanese translation of the abstract see Supplementary Materials section.

title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Analog-Type Amyloidosis: A Case Report and Review of the Literature.
abstract: Amyloidosis is a heterogeneous group of diseases characterized by extracellular deposition of insoluble proteins. Glucagon-like peptide-1 analog (AGLP1)-type amyloidosis is a rare iatrogenic form of amyloidosis localized to areas of glucagon-like peptide-1 analog injections. In this study, we describe a case of AGLP1-type amyloidosis presenting as a subcutaneous mass on the abdomen of a 71-year-old woman with a history of liraglutide, semaglutide, and tirzepatide use. Biopsy, including Congo red stain, was consistent with an amyloid deposit. Amyloid protein identification by liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry showed a typical amyloid profile with low spectra for liraglutide. Immunohistochemistry, subsequently performed, showed that the amyloid deposits were positive for glucagon; there is an extensive peptide homology between liraglutide and glucagon. Only 3 cases of AGLP1-type amyloidosis have been previously reported. It is vital for clinicians and pathologists to be aware of AGLP1-type amyloidosis given the increasing worldwide use of GLP-1 agonists, as well as the potential for misdiagnosis of systemic amyloidosis, which has profound therapeutic and prognostic implications.

title: Combined time-restricted feeding and resistance training enhance tirzepatide-induced improvements in adiposity and whole-body insulin sensitivity in female mice.
authors: da Conceição de Mattis Luciana Renata
abstract: Tirzepatide is a dual agonist of glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptors with potent effects on body weight regulation, glucose homeostasis and metabolic health. However, its interaction with dietary and exercise interventions as well as its impact on obesity and hepatic metabolic pathways, particularly in females, remain unclear. Here, we tested whether tirzepatide, alone or combined with time-restricted feeding (TRF) or resistance training, modulates energy balance, strength performance, adipose tissue remodelling, insulin sensitivity and hepatic lipid accumulation in female mice. Female Swiss mice after 10 weeks of obesity induction were treated with tirzepatide, TRF or resistance training for 8 weeks. Tirzepatide was administered subcutaneously using a dose-escalation protocol. TRF consisted of a 12 h feeding window, and resistance training was performed as stair climbing on alternating days. Body weight, caloric intake and feed efficiency were monitored longitudinally. Glucose homeostasis was assessed by intraperitoneal glucose and insulin tolerance tests. Adipose depots, skeletal muscle and liver mass were quantified, and hepatic lipid accumulation was evaluated by histology and RT-qPCR of lipogenic metabolism genes. Tirzepatide reduced body weight gain and feed efficiency, consistent with a negative energy balance. When combined with TRF and resistance training, tirzepatide accelerated weight loss, and the addition of resistance training further enhanced this effect, bringing body weight close to control levels. These effects were associated with reduced adipose mass and adipocyte hypertrophy, indicating improved adipose tissue remodelling. Resistance training improved strength performance and increased skeletal muscle mass. Tirzepatide combined with TRF, with or without resistance training, improved glucose tolerance in female mice. All interventions reduced hepatic lipid accumulation. Collectively, tirzepatide, particularly in combination with TRF and resistance training, exerts enhanced metabolic benefits on obesity, insulin sensitivity and metabolic regulation in female mice. KEY POINTS: Tirzepatide combined with time-restricted feeding and resistance training produced greater reductions in body weight and adiposity in obese female mice. Combined interventions improved whole-body insulin sensitivity more effectively than isolated strategies. Resistance training preserved skeletal muscle mass during tirzepatide-induced weight loss. All interventions similarly reduced hepatic lipid accumulation and lipogenic gene expression. Tirzepatide-based therapies enhanced systemic metabolic health without additional hepatic benefits from combined interventions.

title: Early Treatment Trajectory and Long-Term Persistence to Semaglutide for Obesity: A Population-Based Cohort Study.
abstract: To assess semaglutide persistence in obesity management, identify factors associated with discontinuation and examine early tirzepatide adoption. This retrospective cohort study used Clalit Health Services records of adults without diabetes initiating Wegovy between January and May 2025. Discontinuation was defined as a gap exceeding 60 days after medication coverage ended. Multivariable Cox models, including a Day-90 landmark analysis, assessed discontinuation. Tirzepatide adoption was evaluated following its December 2025 coverage introduction. Among 34 309 participants (67.0% women; mean age 44.6 years), cumulative discontinuation reached 36.5% at 180 days and 67.6% at 365 days. Arab population sector (hazard ratio [HR] 1.65, 95% CI 1.59-1.72), low socioeconomic status (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.09-1.17) and current smoking (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.09-1.17) were associated with discontinuation. In the day-90 landmark cohort (n = 28 218), remaining on 0.25 versus 1.0 mg was associated with subsequent discontinuation (HR 1.88, 95% CI 1.72-2.06), substantially attenuated after adjustment for early refill adherence. Each percentage-point smaller BMI reduction was associated with 3% higher discontinuation hazard (HR 1.03, 95% CI 1.03-1.04). Following tirzepatide availability, 2908 of 33 936 eligible participants (8.6%) initiated treatment over a median 3.1-month observation period. Adoption was associated with higher socioeconomic status and baseline BMI. Semaglutide discontinuation was common and associated with sociodemographic and early treatment characteristics. Day-90 dose and early weight-loss response may help identify discontinuation risk. Socioeconomic differences suggest inequalities in sustained obesity pharmacotherapy access.

title: Neuropsychiatric Safety of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and Tirzepatide in Adults with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus or Obesity.
abstract: Neuropsychiatric safety concerns about glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and tirzepatide prompted regulatory review by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). We synthesized the contemporary evidence in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus or obesity, emphasizing study design, risk of bias, and the distinction between signal detection and causal inference. The PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus databases were searched without a lower date limit through March 15, 2026 (English, adults ≥18 years). The review was reported with reference to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020, and the PRISMA-S and PRISMA-Harms extensions. Evidence was grouped into prespecified categories: randomized syntheses, comparative observational studies and target-trial emulations, outlier non-active-comparator studies, pharmacovigilance analyses, and regulatory reviews. Risk of bias was appraised with the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool and with Risk of Bias in Non-randomised Studies of Interventions; certainty was summarized using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation. Twenty studies and two regulatory reviews met the inclusion criteria. Randomized evidence, including two large 2025 meta-analyses and post hoc pooled analyses of semaglutide and tirzepatide, showed no increased risk of suicidality, depression, or anxiety, though psychiatric exclusion criteria limited generalizability. Active-comparator cohorts from the United States, Scandinavia, and the United Kingdom likewise showed no clear increase after confounding control. Passive-comparator and disproportionality analyses generated signals but could not separate drug effects from baseline psychiatric risk, obesity-related distress, or reporting bias. The EMA and FDA conclusions do not support a causal class-wide association between GLP-1 RAs and suicidal ideation or behavior. Evidence does not support a clinically meaningful increase in neuropsychiatric harm with GLP-1 RAs or tirzepatide in the populations studied. Surveillance remains warranted for patients with substantial psychiatric morbidity, for obesity-only populations, and for long-term rare outcomes.

title: Comparative adverse-event reporting patterns of semaglutide and tirzepatide: a disproportionality analysis of FAERS.
abstract: Semaglutide and tirzepatide are widely used for type 2 diabetes and obesity, but comparative post-marketing safety data remain limited. To compare adverse-event reporting patterns for semaglutide and tirzepatide in the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), focusing on gastrointestinal, renal and ocular events, alopecia, serious outcomes, mortality, and reporting chronology. This retrospective pharmacovigilance study analyzed FAERS reports submitted from January 2022 through June 2026. After deduplication, 215,337 unique reports remained; predefined exposure criteria identified 60,423 semaglutide-only reports, 143,126 tirzepatide-only reports, and 853 reports listing both drugs without additional suspect active ingredients. Disproportionality was assessed using reporting odds ratios (RORs) with 95% confidence intervals. Multivariable logistic regression, false discovery rate adjustment, and reporting-latency analyses were also performed. Semaglutide showed higher reporting odds than tirzepatide for impaired gastric emptying (ROR 6.39), intestinal obstruction/ileus (ROR 4.56), acute kidney injury (ROR 2.51), pancreatitis (ROR 2.18), vomiting (ROR 2.11), and optic ischaemic neuropathy (ROR 15.77). Alopecia was relatively more frequently reported with tirzepatide (ROR 0.74). Semaglutide reports had higher adjusted reporting odds of hospitalization (aOR 2.80) and death (aOR 1.21). In an exploratory analysis restricted to male reports, erectile dysfunction was reported in 92 of 16,673 semaglutide reports and 46 of 27,321 tirzepatide reports (ROR 3.29, 95% CI 2.31-4.69; q < 0.001). Semaglutide and tirzepatide exhibited distinct post-marketing reporting patterns. The erectile-dysfunction finding was exploratory and hypothesis-generating. All findings reflect spontaneous reporting rather than comparative clinical risk or causality and require confirmation in population-based studies.

title: Switching between semaglutide and tirzepatide in obesity management: an expert-consensus framework for approximate clinical efficacy-matched switching doses.
abstract: Currently, there are no available guidelines for switching from semaglutide to tirzepatide, since the mechanisms of action and pharmacokinetics differ, thus posing a challenge for continuous treatment of obesity. A narrative review of PubMed, Embase, and ClinicalTrials.gov (to May 2026) evaluated trials and cohorts comparing semaglutide (0.25-7.2 mg) and tirzepatide (2.5-15 mg). We synthesized indirect treatment comparisons to outline dose-response relationships and develop approximate efficacy‑matched switching dose bands. Estimation of clinical efficacy-matched switching doses is more practical than mandatory lowest-dose initiation, which naturally risks a 'therapeutic gap' and subsequent weight regain. Until prospective switching trials validate exact conversions, clinicians should utilize the proposed equivalence bands and the five-step clinical decision algorithm to guide seamless transitions, titrating doses every 4-8 weeks based on individual tolerability and metabolic outcomes.

title: Tirzepatide Use Resulted in Clinically Meaningful Weight Reduction in Individuals With Obesity or Overweight: 12-Month Real-World Results.
abstract: This study assessed the real-world effectiveness of tirzepatide in commercially insured individuals without diabetes, eligible for obesity medications (OMs), including glucagon like-peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA)-naïve individuals (i.e., no GLP-1 RA prescription during the 12-month pre-index period) and GLP-1 RA-experienced individuals. This retrospective, observational cohort study used Optum's de-identified Market Clarity Data (Optum Market Clarity). Adults with ≥ 1 prescription claim for tirzepatide between November 2023 and March 2024, with continuous medical/pharmacy enrollment for ≥ 12 months pre-index and post-index and available pre- and post-index data were included. Baseline demographics, clinical characteristics, and treatment effectiveness (change from baseline in weight, body mass index, and cardiometabolic risk factors) were assessed among OM-eligible individuals who were persistent on tirzepatide for ≥ 12 months. The GLP-1 RA-naïve and experienced cohorts included 230 individuals (mean age: 49.5 years, 72.2% female) and 123 individuals (mean age: 48.9 years, 81.3% female), respectively, who were persistent on tirzepatide for 12 months with documented pre- and post-index weight measurements. At baseline, more than 85% of individuals in each cohort had ≥ 1 obesity-related complication, most commonly dyslipidemia, hypertension, and prediabetes. At 12 months post-index, the GLP-1 RA-naïve cohort achieved a mean weight reduction of 19.3%, while the GLP-1 RA-experienced cohort achieved a mean weight reduction of 13.1%. After 12 months of persistent tirzepatide use, individuals experienced clinically meaningful weight reduction, comparable to outcomes reported in clinical trials. These real-world findings were observed both in GLP-1 RA-naïve and experienced individuals.

title: The Impact of Incretin-Based Therapies on Anthropometric and Metabolic Parameters in Women with Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome.
journal: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy
abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), recently renamed polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), affects 170 million women globally and is often accompanied by obesity and various levels of insulin resistance. Incretin-based therapies, including the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists liraglutide and semaglutide, and the dual GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) agonist tirzepatide, offer a biologically plausible mechanism for targeting metabolic dysfunction in PMOS. This review examines clinical trial evidence on the anthropometric and metabolic effects of incretin-based therapies in this population, including a focus on women of reproductive age, who face distinct challenges related to preconception planning, treatment duration, and post-discontinuation metabolic and weight management. Available literature shows that liraglutide, semaglutide and tirzepatide produce clinically meaningful reductions in body weight, body mass index (BMI), and waist circumference, with some studies also confirming preferential effects on visceral and ectopic fat compartments. Glycaemic and insulin resistance outcomes vary across studies, while lipid and blood pressure effects remain incompletely characterized. Although emerging data suggest that higher-potency agents may yield more consistent weight-loss benefits, available PMOS-specific evidence does not establish comparative metabolic superiority among agents. Interpretation of the available evidence is limited by the predominance of short-term trials at sub-obesity doses, frequent co-administration with metformin, and the absence of phenotype-stratified data, leaving the full metabolic potential of these agents in PMOS incompletely defined. Larger, longer, and higher-dose trials are needed to fully characterize the anthropometric and metabolic potential of these agents in PMOS.

title: Pancreatic and Gallbladder Adverse Events Associated with Tirzepatide in Obesity Management: A Scoping Review.
journal: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy
abstract: Obesity is a chronic and relapsing condition that affects all demographics and results in comorbidities, rising healthcare costs, and social challenges. Tirzepatide, a novel dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist, has emerged as a promising therapy offering significant weight reduction. However, uncertainty remains regarding its pancreatic and gallbladder safety profile across different populations and evidence sources. To systematically map existing evidence on the safety of tirzepatide in obesity management, with an emphasis on pancreatic- and gallbladder-related adverse events (AEs) across randomized controlled trials (RCTs), observational studies, case reports, and pharmacovigilance evidence. Following the methodological framework of Arksey and O'Malley (2005), expanded with Joanna Briggs Institute guidance, this scoping review included RCTs, observational studies, and post-marketing safety reports identified between December 2019 and September 2025. The searches were conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, and the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), with additional evidence identified through gray literature, targeted journal searches, and published pharmacovigilance studies based on the EudraVigilance database. ClinicalTrials.gov was subsequently searched as an additional source to identify relevant clinical trials. Studies were eligible if they examined pancreatic or gallbladder AEs in the context of tirzepatide exposure among individuals with obesity. The review included 11 RCTs, 5 observational studies, 4 case reports, 1 EudraVigilance pharmacovigilance analysis, and 575 FAERS reports. Pancreatic and gallbladder AEs were systematically extracted and coded using MedDRA version 28.1, following the predetermined hierarchy. Findings were mapped descriptively across data sources without formal comparative statistical testing. Pancreatic and gallbladder AEs were reported infrequently in RCTs. Pancreatitis was reported in 11 participants across five RCTs, with study-specific frequencies ranging from 0.2% (3 of 1,896) to 3.7% (1 of 27), while cholelithiasis was reported in 73 participants across 11 RCTs, with frequencies ranging from 0.3% (1 of 335 and 1 of 364) to 3.7% (1 of 27). Among observational studies, pancreatitis was reported in three studies, with proportions of 0.6% (63/10,002), 0.9% (1/110), and 2.1% (5,882/280,094). One retrospective cohort study reported an incidence rate of 3.84 events per 1,000 person-years among 9,193 participants, while cholelithiasis was reported at 11.89 events per 1,000 person-years in the same cohort. In the EudraVigilance pharmacovigilance analysis, pancreatitis represented 363 reported AEs (6.3% of all AEs and 19.4% of gastrointestinal AEs). In the FAERS database, pancreatitis accounted for 155/288 pancreatic-related reports [53.8%] and cholelithiasis for 143/249 gallbladder-related reports [57.4%]. Four case reports described six distinct AEs: edematous pancreatitis, acute pancreatitis, pancreatitis necrotizing, acalculous cholecystitis, gallstones, and gallbladder wall thickening, each reported once. Female participants, White participants, adults aged 18-64 years, and participants from the United States (US) predominated among reported demographic characteristics; however, demographic characteristics and comorbidity profiles were inconsistently reported and varied across studies. Pancreatic and gallbladder AEs were reported across clinical trials, observational studies, case reports, and pharmacovigilance databases. RCTs generally reported low frequencies of pancreatobiliary AEs, whereas pharmacovigilance databases captured a broader spectrum of reported events. Variability in study populations, comorbidity profiles, reporting methods, and the absence of exposure denominators limited direct comparison across evidence sources. Vigilant monitoring and standardized AE reporting are needed to further characterize the pancreatobiliary safety profile of tirzepatide.

title: GLP-1-Based Therapy in Type 1 Diabetes: Balancing Efficacy, Safety, and Patient Selection.
abstract: To critically examine the evolving evidence on glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and the dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1 receptor agonist tirzepatide as adjuncts to insulin therapy in type 1 diabetes (T1D), with particular emphasis on their benefit-risk balance in individuals with overweight or obesity. This narrative review examines evidence on liraglutide, semaglutide and tirzepatide in T1D, focusing on effects on body weight and insulin requirements, alongside hypoglycaemia, ketosis, diabetic ketoacidosis and gastrointestinal tolerability. Early trials with liraglutide demonstrated reductions in body weight and insulin requirements but raised concerns regarding hypoglycaemia and ketosis. More recently, semaglutide and tirzepatide have renewed interest in incretin-based therapy in T1D, particularly among individuals with obesity. Their greater effects on weight and insulin requirements introduce a clinically important safety challenge: insulin must be reduced sufficiently to prevent hypoglycaemia while maintaining adequate insulinization to suppress lipolysis and ketogenesis. Gastrointestinal adverse events may further destabilize this balance through reduced carbohydrate intake and dehydration. Current evidence supports a phenotype-directed approach centred primarily on adults with T1D and obesity, accompanied by careful patient selection, individualised insulin adjustment, glucose and ketone monitoring, and structured patient education. The clinical question has shifted from whether GLP-1-based therapies are effective in T1D to which patients are most likely to achieve a favourable benefit-risk balance and how these therapies can be used safely.

title: Interpreting Diabetic Retinal Outcomes After GLP-1 Receptor Agonist and Tirzepatide Initiation: Clinical Evidence and Its Limits.
abstract: Reports of diabetic retinopathy after potent glucose-lowering treatment create uncertainty for clinicians, particularly when studies measure different outcomes in patients with different baseline retinal disease. This review examines diabetic retinal outcomes after glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist or tirzepatide initiation. This critical narrative review uses targeted, non-systematic study selection. It distinguishes disease onset or progression from detection, treatment use and subsequent visual function. The SUSTAIN-6 retinopathy-complication signal remains clinically relevant; post hoc associations with early glycated haemoglobin reduction do not establish causal mediation. Contemporary cohorts report differing associations across baseline retinal strata, comparators and endpoints. Positive signals should be presented alongside their absolute event proportions and limitations, rather than dismissed because observational adjustment is imperfect. Conversely, non-significant results do not establish equivalence or class-wide safety. Current guidance supports establishing retinal status and coordinating diabetes and eye care during treatment intensification. The implications differ between patients with recent screening and no known retinopathy, established non-proliferative disease, and active sight-threatening disease or recent retinal treatment. No universal safe rate of glycated haemoglobin decline or retinal-protective titration regimen has been established. Future studies should align eligibility and treatment initiation, distinguish incident disease from progression, and use scheduled retinal assessments. A comparison between two specific medicines can inform treatment choice but cannot exclude risks shared by both.

title: Oral Health-Related Adverse Events of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.
abstract: As the clinical use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) continues to grow for the management of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular and renal protection, noncirrhotic fatty liver disease, and weight management, their potential implications for oral health need to be considered. This study examined oral health-related adverse events (AEs) associated with GLP-1 RAs using postmarketing data from the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS). FAERS reports for available GLP-1 RAs, exenatide, liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide, and tirzepatide, were screened from their initial market introduction through December 2025, identifying 364,274 total AE reports, of which 31,195 (8.6%) involved oral, craniofacial, or dental manifestations. Tirzepatide, despite being one of the most recently approved GLP-1 RAs, accounted for the highest overall AE volume, and semaglutide demonstrated the largest proportion of oral health-related AEs. A disproportionality analysis revealed a significant drug-specific signal for dry mouth of semaglutide, while vomiting, regurgitation, and reflux-related events produced a significant signal across all 5 drugs. Sensory disorders, including dysgeusia and taste disturbances, also demonstrated significant proportional reporting ratios (PRRs) and reporting odds ratios (RORs) for several GLP-1 RAs. Association analysis of AEs showed significant associations between vomiting and taste disturbances, as well as between dry mouth and dysgeusia, particularly with semaglutide and dulaglutide. This analysis highlights emerging safety signals in oral health and underscores the need for heightened clinical awareness and prospective studies to characterize the incidence, timing, and mechanisms of oral AEs associated with GLP-1 RA therapy.Knowledge Transfer Statement:Understanding the oral adverse effects associated with GLP-1 receptor agonists allows clinicians and dental providers to more effectively counsel patients initiating or continuing these medications. By recognizing early symptoms such as dry mouth, dysgeusia, and reflux-related irritation, providers can implement targeted preventive strategies-including hydration guidance, salivary substitutes, dietary modifications, and closer oral health monitoring-to reduce complications and improve patient comfort, adherence, and overall treatment outcomes. This knowledge enhances interdisciplinary management of individuals using GLP-1 RAs.

title: Glucagon-like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Heart Transplant Recipients With Type 2 Diabetes: A Multicenter Study.
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is frequent after heart transplantation (HT) and is exacerbated by immunosuppressive therapy. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) may improve metabolic control, but data in HT recipients are limited. We performed a retrospective, multicenter study including HT recipients with T2DM from 14 Spanish centers. In patients treated with GLP-1 RAs, we assessed antidiabetic and immunosuppressive therapies, adverse events, and changes in metabolic parameters, insulin dose, and immunosuppressant trough levels during the first year after GLP-1 RA initiation. Among 734 HT recipients with T2DM (2011-2021), 108 (14.7%) received GLP-1 RAs (mean age 55.4 ± 9.0 y; 79.6% male), initiated 4.0 ± 3.1 y post-HT. At baseline, 64.8% had obesity. Semaglutide was used in 59%, dulaglutide in 27%, liraglutide in 13%, and tirzepatide in 1%; 41.7% achieved the maximum therapeutic dose. After 1 y, significant reductions were observed in body weight (-6.2 kg; 95% confidence interval [CI], -7.7 to -4.5 kg), fasting glucose (-27 mg/dL; 95% CI, -41 to -7 mg/dL), glycated hemoglobin (-0.74%; 95% CI, -1.12% to -0.35%), total cholesterol (-12 mg/dL; 95% CI, -19 to -6 mg/dL), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (-8 mg/dL; 95% CI, -14 to -2 mg/dL), triglycerides (-29 mg/dL; 95% CI, -53 to -5 mg/dL), and systolic blood pressure (-3.6 mm Hg; 95% CI, -6.4 to -0.9 mm Hg). Tacrolimus trough levels decreased modestly (-0.7 ng/mL; 95% CI, -1.4 to -0.1 ng/mL; P = 0.025), without episodes of acute rejection. Gastrointestinal adverse events occurred in 12.0%, leading to discontinuation in 3.7%. In HT recipients with T2DM, GLP-1 RAs were associated with improved glycemic and cardiometabolic parameters and were generally well tolerated. These findings support the use of GLP-1 RAs as a valuable therapeutic strategy for the management of T2DM after HT.

title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists and Risk of Arrhythmias: A Network Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Arrhythmias are often associated with comorbidities such as diabetes and obesity, which significantly influence their onset and progression. In this context, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have garnered attention for their potential benefits, with emerging evidence indicating that GLP-1 receptor activation might offer antiarrhythmic effects. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of all GLP-1 RAs and co-agonists on the incidence of new-onset arrhythmias, particularly atrial fibrillation (AF). A comprehensive search of databases was conducted from inception to December 2025. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) focusing on patients with diabetes or obesity receiving GLP-1 RAs or co-agonists.
